notes: “Wife of prostitution” and “children of prostitution” retain the Hebrew’s force. The wording does not settle when Gomer became sexually unfaithful or establish the children’s paternity. The marriage functions as a prophetic sign concerning the land.
The final clause is difficult. This draft reads it as refusal to forgive within the preceding negative statement; “I will certainly take them away” is another understanding.
“I will not be yours” preserves the terse covenant reversal. Verses 10–11 are 2:1–2 in the Hebrew source; the restoration follows the judgment without an added transition scene.
vocabulary: “God sows”; also the place associated with the bloodshed named here. Its meaning becomes hopeful in 2:22–23.
“Not Shown Compassion”; “Not My People.” Their meanings are reversed in the restoration sayings.

notes: The speaker’s threatened stripping, deprivation, and killing belong to the poem’s portrayal of the broken relationship with the land and its people. The translation preserves the harm and does not present it as guidance for marriage.
The Hebrew shifts between direct address and third-person description, and between feminine and masculine collective figures. Those shifts have been retained where English permits.
Achor means “trouble.” “Respond” in verse 15 can also be understood as singing. Baal can mean “master” or “husband” as well as naming a god, which makes the change of address in verse 16 significant.
The covenant explicitly includes wild animals, birds, and ground-dwelling creatures. Its peace is not restricted to human relationships.
vocabulary: Hesed: steadfast kindness and loyalty within a relationship.
The repeated verb links God, skies, earth, crops, and Jezreel in a chain of restored provision.

notes: The woman is unnamed here. “Loved by another man” follows the pointed Hebrew; different pointing can yield a different description. The purchase does not specify a legal setting, and the final reciprocal promise is terse.
“David their king” is the source’s expression. The verse does not name a particular later ruler.
vocabulary: Dry measures: the lethek is commonly understood as half a homer. Exact modern capacities are uncertain.
Objects associated with priestly or divinatory practice. Their absence is listed alongside the loss of kingship and sacrifice.

notes: Verse 4 follows the transmitted comparison with people who contend against a priest; its syntax is disputed. Verse 7 retains God as the one exchanging honor for shame, rather than substituting another textual reading.
“Sin” can also mean a sin offering, giving “feed on sin” a pointed double sense. The end of verse 10 is difficult and may be connected differently with verse 11.

The Hebrew calls the women qedeshot, women set apart in a religious setting. Their precise role is uncertain; the translation does not assume a settled category of temple prostitution. The men’s conduct is explicitly part of the accusation.

The pasture clause can be read as a question or a statement. Verse 18 has compressed and unusual wording; the draft preserves the rulers’ attachment to disgrace without claiming certainty about each phrase.
vocabulary: “House of wickedness” or “worthlessness,” used polemically in the setting of worship associated with Bethel.
The name of a tribe, frequently used here for the northern kingdom of Israel.

sections.1: The LORD’s case against the land

notes: These lines are difficult: “rebels” and “slaughter,” the devouring “new moon,” and following a “command” preserve readings of the transmitted words. The draft does not silently replace them with proposed emendations.

“Behind you, Benjamin!” is an abrupt alarm whose precise force is uncertain. “Contending king” renders the unusual epithet yareb; it may be understood as a title or differently divided wording, rather than a known personal name.
vocabulary: Markers of inherited land; moving them wrongfully takes another person’s property.

notes: The communal appeal is followed by God’s challenge in verse 4. The text does not label the appeal as either fully sincere or merely presumptuous. The two-day/third-day language remains in its own setting.

Verse 5 follows “your judgments,” understood as judgments against the addressees. “Like Adam” may refer to Adam, humanity, or a place named Adam; “there” makes the place interpretation possible, but the text remains uncertain.
The final temporal clause can be connected with what precedes or with 7:1. This draft lets the sentence continue across the chapter boundary.
vocabulary: An offering wholly burned on the altar.
A named city; the accusation concerns murder on the road leading there.

notes: The oven and baker form an extended image of heated plotting. Verse 6 preserves “their baker,” though the wording and some pronoun references are difficult.

The congregation’s hearing in verse 12 is obscure. Verse 14 follows gathering rather than an emendation to self-cutting. “Not upward” in verse 16 preserves the terse wording; “not to the Most High” is an interpretation of it.
vocabulary: Bread left cooked on one side and uncooked on the other; the image exposes Ephraim’s condition without an added abstract label.
Secure release or rescue from another’s power.

notes: The subject of “rejected” in verse 5 is uncertain, so English uses a passive clause. The gathering and royal burden in verse 10 are also difficult; the draft does not name an unstated monarch.
The repeated “sin” can also evoke sin offerings. Verse 12 describes abundant written instruction being treated as foreign; its verbal forms permit more than one temporal nuance.
vocabulary: A crafted image associated with worship in the northern kingdom.
The linked agricultural verbs picture consequences far greater than what was planted.

notes: The source does not mark quotation boundaries. This draft treats “The prophet is a fool” as hostile speech and the prophet as a watchman; other parses make the prophet himself part of the indictment.

Verse 13 retains the difficult reference to Tyre. The following prayer and judgment explicitly concern miscarriage, bereavement, and the death of children; they have not been softened into general hardship.
vocabulary: Food associated with mourning and ritual impurity, unsuitable for sanctuary use in this description.
The place or worship associated with the remembered breach of loyalty; “Shame” is a contemptuous designation in the verse.

notes: The heart can be described as false or divided. Verse 5 moves from plural calves to a singular image. The floating object in verse 7 may be a twig or foam.

The Gibeah clause is difficult; this draft reads a rhetorical question. Verse 10 follows the traditional read form “offenses.” The neck clause in verse 11 is not fully explained. The final verb of verse 12 may mean rain or teach righteousness.
Shalman and Beth-arbel are retained without a firm identification. The family killings and the source’s naming of Bethel as responsible remain explicit.
vocabulary: Land that must be broken up before sowing; the farming image describes a needed change in conduct.

notes: Verse 2 has plural callers, without naming them. The arms phrase in verse 3 is difficult; this draft relates the arms to Ephraim. Verse 4 follows the pointed “yoke,” not a repointed word for an infant.

Several lines resist a single clear reading. The negative about Egypt is retained. “Upward” in verse 7 and “city” in verse 9 follow the transmitted wording; “wrath” is another proposed understanding of verse 9. Verse 12 can be read as criticizing Judah’s restlessness or contrasting Judah’s faithfulness; the draft’s reading remains provisional.
vocabulary: Cities remembered among those destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah.
The repeated verb joins awe and the urgent movement home.

sections.8: How can I give you up?

notes: The Jacob sayings echo heel-grasping, struggle, and Bethel, but the subjects of some “he/him” clauses are uncertain. The source says God spoke “with us,” not only with Jacob.
The word for merchant is also “Canaan.” The tents evoke an appointed festival but may also suggest renewed wilderness life. Gilgal and “heaps” sound alike in Hebrew.
vocabulary: A title of divine command over hosts or armies.
Jacob guards flocks; a prophet guards Israel. The repeated root links the ancestral and national stories.

notes: The phrase may mean human sacrificers or sacrificers of human beings. This draft takes it as people who offer sacrifice; the more disturbing alternative remains possible.

Verse 9’s syntax is obscure. In verse 14, the opening lines can be promises of rescue or questions refusing it. This draft uses questions in the immediate judgment context; later uses of the verse do not erase that ambiguity.
The explicit killing of children and pregnant women is part of the announced catastrophe. This verse is 14:1 in the pinned Hebrew source.
vocabulary: The bundle image pictures guilt retained for reckoning, not forgotten.
The realm of the dead, personified here alongside Death.

notes: The pinned Hebrew says “bulls” and “our lips.” The image treats spoken response as an offering. “Fruit of our lips” reflects a different textual understanding and is not silently substituted.
The shade’s referent and the speakers in verse 8 are not fully marked. This draft reads verse 8 as God’s speech; it can also be understood as a dialogue with Ephraim.
vocabulary: Willingly, without compulsion; the word describes the love promised here.
Paths of life and conduct; the same paths are walked by the righteous and stumbled over by rebels.
